title: She Was Dropped Twice. Smriti Mandhana Made Pakistan Pay With 68 Off 44 at Edgbaston.
excerpt: Mandhana's fifth fifty in T20 World Cups ties Mithali Raj and Harmanpreet Kaur as India crush Pakistan by 64 runs to open their campaign
body:
She walked in at 18 for 2. Shafali Verma was gone. Jemimah Rodrigues had followed. Pakistan's seamers had found movement under Edgbaston's overcast sky, and India's chase for a statement opening to the Women's T20 World Cup was on the verge of becoming an early crisis.

Smriti Mandhana had other plans.

The left-hander played with the composure of someone who has been here before — because she has. Over 44 balls, Mandhana assembled an innings of 68 that was equal parts elegance and authority: nine fours, two sixes, and a fifty reached off just 34 deliveries. It was the foundation upon which India built 170 for 6 and then dismantled Pakistan for 106, winning by 64 runs.

## Two Lives, One Lesson

Mandhana was dropped twice — at 24 by one fielder in the deep, and again at 55 when Saira Jabeen failed to hold on at the boundary. Pakistan paid dearly. Both reprieves came off edges and miscues, the sort of chances that vanish in a World Cup. Mandhana made them vanish in the only way that mattered: by converting each reprieve into runs.

Her partnership with captain Harmanpreet Kaur — 91 runs off 64 balls for the third wicket — was the decisive passage of the innings. Harmanpreet, who contributed a characteristically punchy 36, rotated the strike with purpose while Mandhana anchored. Together, they shifted the momentum so thoroughly that when Richa Ghosh arrived late to smash 34 off 17, the total had already moved beyond Pakistan's comfort.

## A Record Alongside the Greats

The fifty was Mandhana's fifth score of 50 or more in Women's T20 World Cups. That ties her with Mithali Raj (who needed 23 innings) and Harmanpreet Kaur (34 innings). Mandhana reached the mark in her 26th — the most efficient of the three.

For a player whose T20 World Cup narrative has been defined more by what India have not won than by what she has done, the numbers tell a quieter truth. Mandhana averages in the low twenties across T20 World Cups, but her impact at the top of the order has been outsized. When she scores, India tend to win. This is not coincidence.

## The Collapse That Followed

What Mandhana set up, Deepti Sharma finished. Pakistan's chase was alive at 37 without loss off four overs before Sharma's introduction changed everything. The off-spinner returned figures of 5 for 10 — career-best in T20Is — and alongside Shree Charani (3 for 21) reduced Pakistan from promise to wreckage.

Muneeba Ali's 41 was the lone resistance. The rest of the batting order managed 65 between them, with four batters failing to reach double figures.

## Edgbaston, and What Comes Next

The venue was significant. Edgbaston has hosted Mandhana in county cricket for years; she has played for Birmingham Phoenix in The Hundred and trained at this ground through English summers. The crowd of 18,814 — the highest ever for a group-stage match in Women's T20 World Cup history — gave the occasion a semifinal atmosphere from the first ball.

India now face the Netherlands at Headingley, Leeds on Wednesday, June 17, before their toughest group test against South Africa at Old Trafford on June 21. With Australia also in Group A, the path to the semifinals requires consistency, not just flashes of brilliance.

## Why NRIs Should Pay Attention

Mandhana is arguably the most recognisable Indian woman cricketer among diaspora audiences. Her stints in English domestic cricket, her appearances in the Women's Premier League, and her visibility in global brand campaigns have made her the face of Indian women's cricket beyond India. For NRIs in the UK, watching her bat at Edgbaston — a ground many of them have visited for Test matches and county games — carries a resonance that transcends the scorecard.

This T20 World Cup, held entirely in England across Birmingham, Leeds, Manchester, and Southampton, is the most accessible the tournament has ever been for Indian communities in the UK. Tickets are available, the venues are familiar, and the timing — mid-June, with long English evenings — makes attendance straightforward. If Mandhana continues to bat like this, many of those 18,814 will be back.
